summaries.example: Imagine a very powerful builder. Could the builder make a cube that has no shape at all? That request is not just difficult; it seems impossible because a cube must have a shape. Philosophers ask whether being all-powerful means being able to do even impossible things. Many argue that it does not. They say an all-powerful being can do everything that can really be done, but does not need to make contradictions true.
summaries.summary: Omnipotence means having the greatest possible power. The idea is often connected with God, but philosophers first ask what “greatest possible power” could mean. The famous stone puzzle seems to show a problem: if an all-powerful being can make a stone it cannot move, it cannot move that stone; if it cannot make such a stone, there is something it cannot make. One response is that an impossible request is not a genuine task. A cube with no shape is not a real possibility, and an all-powerful being need not do what no agent could do. The entry also explains that power is more than having an ability: it includes having the opportunity to use it. This helps with cases involving the past or another person's free decision. Several more detailed accounts are considered, including accounts based on repeatable situations and on possible worlds that share a history up to a certain time. The entry finally discusses whether an all-powerful being can also be perfectly good. Different philosophers give different answers, and the questions remain difficult.
key_ideas: Omnipotence is usually understood as the greatest possible overall power, not as the ability to make every sentence true.
The stone puzzle asks whether an all-powerful being could make a stone it could not move. Either answer seems to create a limit.
An all-powerful being may not need to change logic, mathematics, the past, or another person's free choice.
Philosophers have proposed different explanations of omnipotence, but the entry examines difficulties with these explanations.
The entry also asks whether more than one all-powerful being could exist at the same time.
Some philosophers argue that divine goodness and omnipotence can fit together because goodness may rule out certain actions without making the being weaker overall.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about omnipotence teaches us to examine big words carefully. “Can do anything” may hide several different ideas: doing every possible thing, being stronger than every other being, or having unlimited power. Sorting these ideas helps us understand arguments about God, goodness, freedom, logic, and time without treating a puzzle as if it already had an easy answer.

important_terms.definition: Having as much power as any being could have; no other being could have greater overall power.
A situation or fact that could be true or could happen.
A situation that cannot be true, such as a cube with no shape at all.
The chance or circumstances needed for an ability to be used. Philosophers say power includes ability plus opportunity.

questions_to_think_about: Is doing something impossible a real kind of power?
Can someone be strongest overall even if another person can do one thing they cannot?
Why might changing the past be different from changing the future?
Could two people with unlimited power ever disagree about what happens?

summaries.example: Consider a being that can move a feather into infinitely many different places but cannot move a boulder. It may have an enormous or even “infinite” ability in one respect, yet it does not seem omnipotent. This example separates quantity from scope: omnipotence is not simply producing an infinite amount of energy or bringing about infinitely many outcomes. It concerns maximal overall power. The entry therefore treats “infinite power” as an inadequate definition unless it explains which kinds of states of affairs fall within that power.
summaries.summary: The entry analyzes omnipotence primarily as maximal power: an agent is omnipotent when no possible being could exceed its overall power. This is different from the stronger claim that the agent can bring about every state of affairs whatsoever. Impossible states of affairs cannot be brought about, and necessary states of affairs do not depend on an agent's action. The stone paradox illustrates why the unrestricted formulation is problematic. The discussion also examines whether an omnipotent agent can alter the past, bring about another agent's libertarian free choice, or create a situation in which it later loses omnipotence. “Infinite power” is considered but found too imprecise: an agent might have infinitely many powers of one type while lacking powers of another type. Two more detailed strategies are examined. One uses unrestricted repeatability, excluding states whose history or structure prevents the kind of control omnipotence requires. The other uses shared histories between possible worlds to assess what an agent can do given the past. Proposed analyses face objections, including cases involving an essentially limited agent and a state of affairs combining an event with the nonexistence of any omnipotent agent. The entry also considers whether divine moral perfection conflicts with omnipotence. On an Anselmian view, morally forbidden or evil states incompatible with a maximally good world may be impossible, so lacking power over them need not undermine maximal power. Other theological views frame the issue differently.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes an absolute notion of omnipotence—power over every state of affairs—from maximal power, which is limited by what is possible.
The stone paradox exposes a tension between creating a stone that cannot be moved and remaining able to move every stone.
An agent need not be able to bring about necessary or impossible states of affairs. The account also considers limits involving the past and libertarian free choice.
Defining omnipotence as “infinite power” is insufficient: infinite energy or infinitely many outcomes need not provide command over every relevant kind of power.
The unrestricted-repeatability approach restricts the required objects of power to states of affairs that are possible and repeatable in a suitable way.
Shared-histories approaches analyze what an agent can do at a time in worlds with the same prior history, though the entry identifies difficulties for proposed versions of these accounts.
summaries.why_it_matters: The analysis shows how metaphysical arguments depend on distinctions that ordinary language often blurs: possible versus impossible, ability versus opportunity, direct versus indirect causation, and overall power versus power of one particular kind. These distinctions matter not only for philosophy of religion but also for reasoning about freedom, responsibility, causation, time, and the limits of coherent concepts.

important_terms.definition: In the comparative sense emphasized in the entry, power that no possible being could exceed overall.
A fact or situation that obtains or fails to obtain; philosophical analyses of power often ask which such situations an agent can bring about.
A condition that must be true and cannot be made true by an agent's action, since it obtains regardless of that action.
A condition that cannot obtain in any possible situation, such as a shapeless cube.
The power to act, together with circumstances that allow the power to be exercised.
A state of affairs that can occur, cease, and occur again without a built-in final limit on repetition.
A possible world that matches another world's history up to a specified time, after which the worlds may differ.
The view that God necessarily exists and necessarily has great-making properties such as omnipotence, knowledge, and moral perfection.

questions_to_think_about: Does maximal overall power require the ability to perform every action another agent can perform?
Should an inability to change the past count as a limitation on omnipotence?
Can a free decision be caused or directly controlled without ceasing to be free?
If moral perfection rules out evil actions, does that reduce power or instead exclude impossible actions?
Would two omnipotent agents inevitably create stalemates if they tried to produce incompatible outcomes?

summaries.example: Suppose a character in a story is called the most powerful character ever. Another character can make a certain small event happen, but the first character cannot make that event happen because doing so would require making an impossible world. Does that make the first character less powerful? The entry's answer is not automatically. Being strongest overall does not mean copying every ability of every other agent. It means having greater total power, while impossible tasks and some tasks involving freedom or the past may not count against that status.
summaries.summary: Omnipotence is often described as being able to do anything, but the entry asks what that phrase should mean. One proposal says it means power over every state of affairs, including logical or mathematical necessities and impossibilities. That proposal appears incoherent: an impossible situation cannot become real simply because someone tries to create it. The entry therefore focuses on maximal power, understood as overall power that no possible being could exceed. This does not require an omnipotent agent to do every single thing another agent can do. It also does not require control over the past or over another person's free decision. The stone riddle shows the problem clearly. If an omnipotent agent can create a stone it cannot move, it lacks the power to move that stone; if it cannot create such a stone, it lacks the power to create that situation. The puzzle may be answered by noting that an essentially omnipotent agent cannot become non-omnipotent, so the proposed stone situation is impossible. The entry examines two more careful approaches. One says that omnipotence concerns suitably possible and unrestrictedly repeatable states of affairs. Another looks at what an agent can do in possible worlds that share its history up to a given time. These theories are more precise but face their own objections. The entry also discusses whether perfect goodness limits divine power and presents competing philosophical responses.
key_ideas: The stone riddle seems to trap omnipotence: either the being can make an unmovable stone or cannot.
Many philosophers solve this by saying that omnipotence covers possible tasks, not contradictions.
The entry separates being able to do something from having the opportunity to do it.
Changing the past and controlling another person's genuinely free choice may be outside an omnipotent agent's power.
An account based only on infinite strength or infinitely many actions is too broad and does not explain the range of powers needed.
Philosophers compare different theories based on repeatable situations and on possible worlds with matching histories.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic is useful because it shows how philosophers test a concept by using difficult examples. It also teaches that “all-powerful” can mean different things: unlimited ability, the ability to perform every possible task, or the greatest overall power. Understanding those differences helps readers evaluate arguments instead of answering a complicated question with a simple slogan.

important_terms.definition: The greatest overall power that any possible being could have.
A condition or event that might be true or happen.
A condition that cannot be true, such as a round square.
A condition that must be true whether or not anyone acts.
Having an ability and also having the chance to use it in the situation.
A situation that can happen again and again, with no required final repetition.
Possible worlds that have the same past up to a particular moment and then may develop differently.

questions_to_think_about: If a task is impossible, should failing to do it count as weakness?
Can someone be the most powerful overall while lacking one ability another person has?
Why might an agent be unable to change something that has already happened?
Would two all-powerful agents be able to stop each other?
Can perfect goodness and maximum power belong to the same being?
